entry.title: 8. Graphs
entry.content:
The unifying idea. A graph is a set of nodes connected by edges. Almost every “model relationships” problem reduces to one of five operations: represent the graph, traverse it (BFS/DFS), order it (topo sort), find cheapest paths (shortest paths), or find the cheapest spanning structure (MST). This sheet covers all five.

Problem shape Operation Section
Model relationships between entities; choose how to store them Representation A
Visit all reachable nodes; find shortest path in unweighted graph; detect cycles BFS / DFS B
Schedule tasks with prerequisites; process in dependency order Topological sort C
Find minimum-cost path from one source to all other nodes Shortest paths D
Connect all nodes with minimum total edge weight, no cycles MST E

A. Graph representations

Why · the right representation determines whether every operation is fast or slow. Where · any graph problem; choose before coding.

A graph \(G = (V, E)\) has vertices \(V\) and edges \(E\). Two standard representations:

Adjacency list — a dict mapping each node to its neighbors. Standard for sparse graphs.

# unweighted directed graph: 0→1, 0→2, 1→3, 2→3, 3→4
graph = {
    0: [1, 2],
    1: [3],
    2: [3],
    3: [4],
    4: [],
}

# weighted: each neighbor is a (node, weight) pair
weighted = {
    0: [(1, 2), (2, 6)],
    1: [(3, 8)],
    2: [(3, 3)],
}

Adjacency matrix — a 2D array where matrix[u][v] holds the edge weight (0 if no edge). Standard for dense graphs or when \(O(1)\) edge lookup is required.

# same graph as a matrix (5 nodes)
matrix = [
    [0, 1, 1, 0, 0],   # node 0
    [0, 0, 0, 1, 0],   # node 1
    [0, 0, 0, 1, 0],   # node 2
    [0, 0, 0, 0, 1],   # node 3
    [0, 0, 0, 0, 0],   # node 4
]

Figure 1 · The same graph as an adjacency list and adjacency matrix.

Orange cells in the matrix mark edges. The list only stores existing edges; the matrix stores all possible pairs — that difference drives the space and lookup costs.

Cost comparison:

  Adjacency list Adjacency matrix
Space \(O(V + E)\) \(O(V^2)\)
Edge lookup (u,v) \(O(\deg(u))\) — scan neighbors \(O(1)\) — direct index
Iterate all edges \(O(V + E)\) \(O(V^2)\)

Use list when the graph is sparse (\(E \ll V^2\)) — most real graphs. Use matrix when \(V\) is small and you need fast edge queries, or when the graph is dense.

B. BFS and DFS

Why · reach all nodes reachable from a source; differ in what order they visit nodes, which determines what each algorithm can guarantee. Where · BFS for shortest paths in unweighted graphs and level-order traversal; DFS for topo sort, cycle detection, and connected components.

Both algorithms visit every reachable node exactly once: \(O(V + E)\) — one pass over each vertex and each edge. The difference is the data structure that controls visit order.

Figure 2 · BFS wavefront vs DFS corridor on the same graph.

BFS (left): expands level by level — all nodes at distance \(k\) before any at \(k+1\). DFS (right): plunges down one path until stuck, then backtracks. Numbers show DFS visit order.

BFS — uses a queue; guarantees shortest path in unweighted graphs.

The queue is FIFO, so all nodes discovered at distance 1 are processed before any at distance 2, and so on. A node is never revisited (if neighbor not in dist prevents it), so its distance is fixed at the first — and therefore minimum — number of hops it took to reach it.

Invariant: all nodes at distance \(k\) from the source are fully processed before any node at distance \(k+1\) is visited.

from collections import deque

def bfs(graph, source):
    dist = {source: 0}
    queue = deque([source])
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        for neighbor in graph[node]:
            if neighbor not in dist:
                dist[neighbor] = dist[node] + 1
                queue.append(neighbor)
    return dist

Mechanism trace on the graph from Figure 2, source = s:

  1. Queue:. Visit s (dist=0). Enqueue a, b.
  2. Queue: [a, b]. Visit a (dist=1). Enqueue c.
  3. Queue: [b, c]. Visit b (dist=1). Enqueue d, e.
  4. Queue: [c, d, e]. Visit c, d, e (dist=2). Queue empty → done.

Cost: \(O(V + E)\) — each node enqueued once, each edge examined once.

DFS — uses recursion (implicit stack); produces finish order used for topo sort.

The call stack naturally goes as deep as possible before backtracking. A node finishes (returns) only after all nodes reachable from it have been fully explored — deeper nodes finish first, shallower nodes last. Section C uses this finish order for topological sort.

Invariant: a node is marked finished only after all nodes reachable from it are finished.

def dfs(graph, source, visited=None):
    if visited is None:
        visited = set()
    visited.add(source)
    for neighbor in graph[source]:
        if neighbor not in visited:
            dfs(graph, neighbor, visited)
    return visited   # reachability only; Section C extends this to record finish order

Mechanism trace on Figure 2, source = s:

  1. Visit s → recurse into a.
  2. Visit a → recurse into c.
  3. Visit c → no unvisited neighbors → c finished.
  4. Back at a → no more neighbors → a finished.
  5. Back at s → recurse into b → visit b, d, e in order → b finished → s finished.

Cost: \(O(V + E)\) — each node visited once, each edge examined once.

  BFS DFS
Data structure Queue Recursion / stack
Order Level by level (wavefront) Deep first (corridor)
Shortest path (unweighted) ✓ ✗
Topo sort / cycle detection ✗ ✓
Connected components ✓ ✓

Note: Floyd’s cycle detection (fast/slow pointer) is a related technique for detecting cycles in linked structures (not a graph traversal algorithm) — see Array & String Techniques.

C. Topological sort

Why · produce a linear ordering of nodes such that for every edge A → B, A appears before B — so no dependency is ever processed before the thing it depends on. Where · task scheduling, dependency resolution, build systems, DAG DP.

A topological order of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a sequence of nodes where every directed edge \(u \to v\) has \(u\) before \(v\). It exists if and only if the graph is a DAG (no cycles).

Intuition — built up step by step:

  • Finish time encodes dependency depth: DFS fully explores a node’s dependencies before marking it finished. Leaf nodes (no outgoing edges) finish first; a source node with many downstream dependencies finishes last, because its entire subtree must complete first.
  • Reverse finish order = topo order: if there is an edge \(u \to v\), DFS finishes \(v\) before \(u\) (it recurses into \(v\) first). Reversing puts \(u\) before \(v\) — exactly the topological requirement.

Invariant: a node appears in the output only after all nodes it depends on have been output.

Figure 3 · Course prerequisite DAG: DFS finish times and one valid topo order.

Diamond shape: A must precede B and C; both B and C must precede D. Two valid orders exist (A→B→C→D or A→C→B→D) — topo sort finds one. Finish times (\(f=\)) annotate each node; reversing them gives the order.

Algorithm:

def topo_sort(graph):
    visited = set()
    result = []

    def dfs(node):
        visited.add(node)
        for neighbor in graph[node]:
            if neighbor not in visited:
                dfs(neighbor)
        result.append(node)          # finish: all dependencies done

    for node in graph:
        if node not in visited:
            dfs(node)
    return result[::-1]             # reverse = topo order

Mechanism trace on Figure 3 (A=Intro CS, B=Algorithms, C=Data Structs, D=Systems Design):

  1. DFS from A → recurse into B → recurse into D.
  2. D has no neighbors → D finishes (f=1). Append D.
  3. Back at B → no more neighbors → B finishes (f=2). Append B.
  4. Back at A → recurse into C → D already visited → C finishes (f=3). Append C.
  5. Back at A → no more neighbors → A finishes (f=4). Append A.
  6. Reverse: [A, B, C, D] — A before B and C, both before D. ✓

B finishes before C only because B appears first in A’s adjacency list — there is no dependency between B and C, so both orderings are equally valid. The algorithm picks one arbitrarily based on iteration order.

Cost: \(O(V + E)\) — one full DFS pass.

[DP expansion — ~2 lines] Topological order enables DAG DP: process nodes in topo order so each node’s subproblem is solved after all its dependencies. Shortest/longest paths in a DAG, counting paths, and many scheduling problems reduce to this. Add memoization here → that’s Dynamic Programming, deliberately deferred from this atlas.

D. Shortest paths

Why · find the minimum-cost path from a source to all other nodes. Where · routing, navigation, network cost optimization, any “minimum cost to reach” problem.

Problem: given a weighted graph \(G = (V, E, w)\) and source node \(s\), find the shortest-path distance \(\delta(s, v)\) from \(s\) to every node \(v \in V\), where \(\delta(s, v)\) is the minimum total weight over all paths from \(s\) to \(v\) (\(\infty\) if \(v\) is unreachable).

Relaxation is the shared core operation across all SSSP algorithms. Every node starts with distance estimate \(d[v] = \infty\) — “I don’t know how to reach you yet” — except the source \(d[s] = 0\). Relaxing edge \((u, v, w)\) asks: “is the path through \(u\) — costing \(d[u] + w\) — cheaper than my current best \(d[v]\)?” If yes, update. Estimates only ever decrease, never overshoot. Repeat until no more updates are possible and every \(d[v]\) converges to \(\delta(s, v)\). The algorithms below differ only in the order they choose to relax edges, which determines their cost and which graphs they handle correctly.

def relax(u, v, w, dist):
    if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:   # cheaper path to v found via u?
        dist[v] = dist[u] + w   # tighten the estimate

Figure 4 · Relaxation on a 3-node graph: the cheaper path via u beats the direct s→v edge.

d[u]=2 was already set via s→u. Relaxing u→v asks: is 2+3=5 cheaper than the current d[v]=8 (set via s→v direct)? Yes → d[v] updates to 5 (orange). The condition and update are identical in every SSSP algorithm — only the order of relaxations differs.

Which algorithm? — depends on the graph type:

Graph type Edge weights Algorithm Cost
Unweighted all = 1 BFS (Section B) \(O(V + E)\)
DAG any DAG relaxation \(O(V + E)\)
General non-negative Dijkstra \(O((V + E) \log V)\)
General any (negative ok) Bellman-Ford \(O(V \cdot E)\)

Dijkstra’s algorithm — general graphs with non-negative weights.

Intuition — built up step by step:

  • The heap is a min-heap of (distance, node) pairs. It starts with just the source at distance 0. The minimum is always at the root, so the next candidate costs \(O(1)\) to read and \(O(\log V)\) to remove (one swap per level as the heap sifts down to restore order).
  • Settling a node means: pop it from the heap, declare its distance final, then relax all its outgoing edges — for each neighbor, check if going through this node beats the current best known distance, and if so push the improved estimate onto the heap.
  • Why the distance is final when settled: the heap always gives the smallest current estimate next. Any future path to this node would go through an unsettled node, which has distance at least as large — so it can only be equal or worse. Negative weights break this: a negative edge discovered later could shorten a distance already declared final.
  • The sphere: settling always expands to the nearest unsettled node, so the settled set grows outward by distance — like a wavefront.

Invariant: once a node is settled, its distance is the true shortest-path distance.

Figure 5 · Dijkstra sphere growing: settled nodes (green), frontier (blue), unseen (grey).

Each panel settles one node (orange border). Distances below each node update as relaxations tighten estimates. The sphere grows outward from s.

Algorithm:

import heapq

def dijkstra(graph, source):
    dist = {node: float("inf") for node in graph}
    dist[source] = 0
    heap = [(0, source)]               # (distance, node)

    while heap:
        d, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if d > dist[node]:
            continue                   # stale entry — already settled
        for neighbor, weight in graph[node]:
            new_dist = dist[node] + weight
            if new_dist < dist[neighbor]:
                dist[neighbor] = new_dist
                heapq.heappush(heap, (new_dist, neighbor))
    return dist

Mechanism trace on Figure 5, edges as shown:

  1. Pop (0,s) → settle s (dist=0): relax a→2, b→6. Heap: [(2,a),(6,b)].
  2. Pop (2,a) → settle a (dist=2): relax b→5 (improves 6→5), c→10. Heap: [(5,b),(6,b),(10,c)].
  3. Pop (5,b) → settle b (dist=5): relax t→12. Heap: [(6,b),(10,c),(12,t)].
  4. Pop (10,c) → settle c (dist=10): relax t→11 (improves 12→11). Heap: [(11,t),(12,t)].
  5. Pop (11,t) → settle t (dist=11). Done. Result: {s:0, a:2, b:5, c:10, t:11}.

(Steps 4–5 skip stale entries (6,b) and (12,t) along the way — nodes already settled get popped and discarded by the if d > dist[node]: continue guard.)

Cost: \(O((V + E) \log V)\) — each node popped once (\(V\) pops), each edge relaxed once (\(E\) pushes), each heap operation costs \(O(\log V)\).

Bellman-Ford — handles negative edge weights; detects negative cycles.

Intuition — built up step by step:

  • No ordering assumption: unlike Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford does not pick the closest node next. It relaxes every edge in the graph, in any order, once per round.
  • Why \(V - 1\) rounds: after round \(k\), every node whose shortest path uses at most \(k\) edges has the correct distance. A simple path (no repeated nodes) uses at most \(V - 1\) edges, so \(V - 1\) rounds guarantee all estimates have converged.
  • Negative cycles: if a \(V\)-th round still relaxes some edge, then there exists a path that keeps getting cheaper by going around a cycle with negative total weight. No finite shortest distance exists in that case.

Invariant: after round \(k\), \(d[v]\) holds the true shortest distance from \(s\) to \(v\) using at most \(k\) edges.

Figure 6 · Bellman-Ford: distance estimates converging over three rounds.

Left: the graph (orange = negative edge). Right: each row is one round; orange cells show updated values. After V−1 rounds all estimates have converged. A further round that still updates signals a negative cycle.

def bellman_ford(nodes, edges, source):
    dist = {node: float("inf") for node in nodes}
    dist[source] = 0

    for _ in range(len(nodes) - 1):    # V-1 rounds
        for u, v, w in edges:          # relax every edge
            if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w

    for u, v, w in edges:              # check for negative cycle
        if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
            raise ValueError("negative cycle detected")
    return dist

Mechanism trace: see Figure 6 — the table shows each round’s updates more clearly than prose steps.

Cost: \(O(V \cdot E)\) — \(V - 1\) rounds each examining all \(E\) edges.

Johnson’s algorithm — all-pairs shortest paths (pointer, not covered in full).

Problem: find \(\delta(u, v)\) for every pair \((u, v) \in V \times V\) — not just from one source.

Why not just run Dijkstra from every node? Dijkstra requires non-negative weights. On graphs with negative edges, running it from every node is incorrect.

Why not run Bellman-Ford from every node? That works but costs \(O(V^2 \cdot E)\) — too slow.

Johnson’s trick — built up step by step:

  • Add a dummy source \(q\) with zero-weight edges to every node. Run Bellman-Ford once from \(q\) to get \(h(v) = \delta(q, v)\) for every node — the potential of \(v\), i.e. its shortest distance from the dummy source.
  • Reweight every edge: \(\hat{w}(u,v) = w(u,v) + h(u) - h(v)\). This shifts the original weight by the difference in shortest-path distances from the dummy source to the two endpoints. The triangle inequality guarantees \(h(v) \leq h(u) + w(u,v)\), so \(\hat{w}(u,v) \geq 0\). Along any path, the \(h\) terms telescope — every intermediate node’s \(h\) cancels between consecutive edges — so all paths between the same pair \((s, t)\) shift by the same constant \(h(s) - h(t)\), preserving which path is shortest.
  • Run Dijkstra from every node on the reweighted graph. Recover original distances: \(\delta(u,v) = \hat{\delta}(u,v) - h(u) + h(v)\).

Cost: \(O(VE)\) for Bellman-Ford + \(O(V \cdot (V+E) \log V)\) for \(V\) Dijkstra runs \(= O(V^2 \log V + VE)\). Running Bellman-Ford from every node would cost \(O(V^2 E)\), so Johnson’s is faster by a factor of \(E / (V \log V + E)\) — most significant on dense graphs where \(E \approx V^2\), giving a factor of \(\approx V\).

E. Minimum spanning tree

Why · connect all nodes with the minimum total edge weight and no cycles — the cheapest network that keeps everything reachable. Where · network design, clustering, Kruskal’s is also the canonical Union-Find application.

A spanning tree of a connected graph is a subset of edges that connects all nodes with no cycles — exactly \(V - 1\) edges for \(V\) nodes. Many spanning trees exist; the minimum one has the smallest total edge weight.

Problem: given a connected undirected weighted graph \(G = (V, E, w)\), find a spanning tree \(T \subseteq E\) that minimises \(\sum_{e \in T} w(e)\).

Figure 7 · A weighted graph (left) and its minimum spanning tree (right).

Left: all edges with weights. Right: the MST (green) connects all 5 nodes with 4 edges at minimum total weight. Dropped edges (grey) would create cycles or aren’t needed.

Two greedy algorithms solve this — each makes one irrevocable choice per step and never backtracks. Greedy works for MST because of the cut property: partition the nodes into any two groups; the cheapest edge crossing that partition must be in the MST. Why? If the MST used a more expensive crossing edge instead, you could swap it for the cheaper one, reduce total weight, and still have a spanning tree — contradicting minimality. This means any algorithm that repeatedly picks the cheapest “safe” edge (one that doesn’t form a cycle) is guaranteed to produce the MST.

Both algorithms below exploit the cut property with a different strategy and a different structure from Hierarchical Structures: Kruskal processes edges globally by weight (Union-Find detects cycles), Prim grows a frontier locally (min-heap picks the cheapest crossing edge).

Kruskal’s algorithm — sort all edges by weight; add each if it doesn’t create a cycle. Uses Union-Find (see Hierarchical Structures Section D) to detect cycles in near-\(O(1)\).

Intuition — built up step by step:

  • Greedy by edge weight: the globally cheapest edge that doesn’t create a cycle is always safe to add to the MST. Processing all edges in sorted order applies this greedily.
  • Cycle detection via Union-Find: two nodes are in the same connected component if they share a root in the Union-Find structure. Adding an edge between two nodes in the same component would close a cycle — skip it.
  • Termination: stop when \(V - 1\) edges have been added. Exactly \(V - 1\) edges connect \(V\) nodes without cycles.

Invariant: the edges added so far form a spanning forest (multiple disconnected trees that haven’t merged yet) of minimum weight — no cheaper set of edges connects the same components. At termination the forest becomes a single spanning tree.

Figure 8 · Kruskal adding edges in sorted order; red = rejected (would create cycle).

Panel 1: first add. Panel 2: (C,D,2) rejected — B, C, D already connected. Panel 3: (A,C,3) connects the isolated node A to the tree. Panel 4: (D,E,5) completes the MST.

def kruskal(nodes, edges):
    parent = {n: n for n in nodes}

    def find(x):
        if parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = find(parent[x])   # path compression
        return parent[x]

    def union(x, y):
        parent[find(x)] = find(y)

    mst = []
    for u, v, w in sorted(edges, key=lambda e: e[2]):
        if find(u) != find(v):            # no cycle
            union(u, v)
            mst.append((u, v, w))
    return mst

Mechanism trace (nodes A–E, same graph as Figure 7):

  1. Sort edges: (B,C,1), (B,D,2), (C,D,2), (A,C,3), (D,E,5), (A,B,4), (C,E,6).
  2. Add (B,C,1) — no cycle. MST: [(B,C,1)].
  3. Add (B,D,2) — no cycle. MST: [(B,C,1),(B,D,2)].
  4. Add (C,D,2) — B,C,D already connected → skip cycle.
  5. Add (A,C,3) — no cycle. MST: [..,(A,C,3)].
  6. Add (D,E,5) — no cycle. MST complete (4 edges for 5 nodes). ✓

Cost: \(O(E \log E)\) — sorting all \(E\) edges costs \(O(E \log E)\); each of the \(E\) Union-Find operations (find + union) costs near-\(O(1)\) amortized with path compression, so sorting dominates.

Prim’s algorithm — grow from one node; always add the cheapest edge crossing the frontier. Uses a min-heap (see Hierarchical Structures Section B).

Intuition — built up step by step:

  • The frontier is the set of edges that cross from the already-settled MST nodes to unsettled nodes. At each step, the cheapest such edge is the safe greedy choice.
  • The heap stores (weight, neighbor, parent) triples for all frontier edges. The root is always the cheapest crossing edge, giving \(O(1)\) access and \(O(\log V)\) removal.
  • Adding a node: pop the cheapest frontier edge, add its target to the MST, then push all edges leaving that newly added node onto the heap as new frontier candidates.
  • Stale entries: a node may appear in the heap multiple times with different weights as better paths are discovered. The if node in in_mst: continue guard skips the stale ones.

Invariant: the settled nodes and their connecting edges always form a minimum spanning tree of the subgraph induced by those nodes.

Figure 9 · Prim growing the MST step by step from node A.

Green = in MST, orange = current frontier edges, blue = not yet reached. Each step the heap picks the cheapest frontier edge and the reached node joins the MST.

def prim(graph, start):
    in_mst = set()
    mst = []
    heap = [(0, start, start)]         # (weight, node, parent)

    while heap:
        w, node, parent = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if node in in_mst:
            continue
        in_mst.add(node)
        if node != start:
            mst.append((parent, node, w))
        for neighbor, weight in graph[node]:
            if neighbor not in in_mst:
                heapq.heappush(heap, (weight, neighbor, node))
    return mst

Mechanism trace on Figure 9, start = A:

  1. Settle A. Frontier: edges to B(4), C(3).
  2. Cheapest crossing edge: (A,C,3). Settle C. Frontier adds B(1 via C), D(2 via C), E(6).
  3. Cheapest: (C,B,1). Settle B. Frontier adds D(2 via B).
  4. Cheapest: (B,D,2) or (C,D,2) — tie, take (B,D,2). Settle D. Frontier adds E(5 via D).
  5. Cheapest: (D,E,5). Settle E. MST complete. ✓

Cost: \(O((V + E) \log V)\) — \(V\) nodes are popped from the heap (one settle per node), and up to \(E\) edges are pushed as frontier candidates. Each push and pop costs \(O(\log V)\), so total: \((V + E) \times O(\log V)\).

Algorithm Approach Key structure Cost
Kruskal Sort edges, add if no cycle Union-Find \(O(E \log E)\)
Prim Grow from one node via frontier Min-heap \(O((V+E) \log V)\)

Use Kruskal when \(E\) is small (sparse graphs) — sorting is cheap and you can enumerate all edges. Use Prim when the graph is dense or already stored as an adjacency list — it settles one node at a time without needing all edges upfront.

🔗 Connections

  • BFS uses deque from Linear Structures; DFS uses recursion stack from Recursion & Backtracking.
  • Dijkstra and Prim use the min-heap from Hierarchical Structures.
  • Kruskal uses Union-Find from Hierarchical Structures.
  • Topo sort enables DAG DP — DP deliberately deferred from this atlas.
  • Shortest-path decision table and graph recognition triggers: the upcoming pattern-triggers post.
  • Floyd’s cycle detection (fast/slow pointer variant of traversal): Array & String Techniques.
  • Kruskal used in MST; merge sort used in edge sorting: Sorting & Searching.

entry.title: 7. Sorting & Searching
entry.content:
The unifying idea. Every algorithm here exploits order: either it creates order (sorting) or it assumes order exists and queries it cheaply (searching). The loop invariant is the tool that makes every loop here correct.

A. Loop invariants — the loop-correctness tool

Why · know a loop is right without tracing it. Where · every loop on this sheet; binary search is the canonical case where getting it wrong causes off-by-ones or infinite loops.

An invariant is a claim about your variables that stays true on every iteration. Prove it holds at the start, each step preserves it, and at termination it gives the result — no tracing required.

Example problem: find the maximum value in a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5].

Invariant: best holds the maximum of all elements seen so far.

a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
best = a[0]           # invariant: best = max(a[0..i])
for x in a[1:]:
    if x > best:
        best = x
# best = 5

Figure 1 · Loop invariant: find-max trace.

best always holds the max of the prefix seen so far. The invariant holds before the loop, after each step, and at termination — so the result is correct by construction.

The three checks:

  • Start: invariant holds before the first iteration.
  • Maintenance: each step preserves the invariant.
  • Termination: invariant + exit condition gives the answer.

The same three checks apply to every loop on this sheet — Section B is the canonical case.

B. Binary search

Why · \(O(\log n)\) find in a sorted array — each step eliminates half the remaining range. Where · any sorted collection; the foundation of Section C’s “binary search on the answer.”

Example problem: find the index of target in sorted nums, or -1 if absent.

Invariant: if the target is present, it lies within nums[left..right]. Every step halves the range while preserving this — off-by-one errors are exactly the bugs that break it.

Algorithm:

nums = [1, 4, 7, 9, 15]
target = 9

left, right = 0, len(nums) - 1   # invariant: if target present, it's in nums[left..right]
while left <= right:
    mid = (left + right) // 2
    if nums[mid] == target:
        result = mid
        break
    elif nums[mid] < target:
        left = mid + 1             # target can't be in [left..mid] — eliminate left half
    else:
        right = mid - 1            # target can't be in [mid..right] — eliminate right half
# result: 3

Figure 2 · Binary search halving: [1,4,7,9,15], target = 9.

Each row is one step. Orange = mid element. Grey = eliminated range. Two steps reach index 3.

Mechanism trace:

  1. left=0, right=4, mid=2, value=7. 9 > 7 → left = 3.
  2. left=3, right=4, mid=3, value=9. Match → found at index 3.

Cost: \(O(\log n)\) — each step halves the remaining range, so after \(k\) steps at most \(\lceil n / 2^k \rceil\) elements remain. The range hits 1 when \(2^k = n\), i.e. \(k = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil\) steps.

Python: bisect.bisect_left(nums, target) for the standard library version.

C. Binary search on the answer

Why · turn “find the minimum \(X\) satisfying a condition” into \(O(\log(\text{range}))\) by binary-searching the answer space instead of the array. Where · capacity/speed/threshold problems where “is \(X\) feasible?” is computable in \(O(n)\).

Invariant: if a valid answer exists, it lies within [left, right] — identical to binary search on an array, but the “array” is the answer space.

The pattern: if a yes/no feasibility question is monotone — once the answer is “yes” for some \(X\), it stays “yes” for all larger \(X\) — binary-search the answer space.

Example problem: given banana piles [3, 6, 7, 11] and hours = 8, find the minimum integer speed (bananas/hour) such that all piles are eaten in time. Each pile takes ⌈pile / speed⌉ hours — you can’t split an hour across piles.

Search range [1, max(piles)]: speed 0 is undefined; at max(piles) every pile takes 1 hour so total = len(piles) ≤ hours — a valid answer always exists. Feasibility is monotone (faster is always at least as good), so binary search on this range finds the minimum valid speed.

Figure 3 · Answer space [1..11]: feasibility above, shrinking search window below.

Top: each circle is one candidate speed; the label shows hours needed. Red = too slow, green = fast enough. The all-red-then-all-green boundary is what makes binary search valid. Bottom: each row is one step — the grey window spans [left, right], the orange tick marks mid, and the window shrinks until only the answer remains.

Algorithm:

piles = [3, 6, 7, 11]
hours = 8

def can_finish(speed):
    return sum((pile + speed - 1) // speed for pile in piles) <= hours

left, right = 1, max(piles)
while left < right:
    mid = (left + right) // 2
    if can_finish(mid):
        right = mid
    else:
        left = mid + 1
# left is the minimum valid speed: 4

Mechanism trace:

  1. left=1, right=11, mid=6. can_finish(6) = 1+1+2+2 = 6 ≤ 8 → right=6.
  2. left=1, right=6, mid=3. can_finish(3) = 1+2+3+4 = 10 > 8 → left=4.
  3. left=4, right=6, mid=5. can_finish(5) = 1+2+2+3 = 8 ≤ 8 → right=5.
  4. left=4, right=5, mid=4. can_finish(4) = 1+2+2+3 = 8 ≤ 8 → right=4.
  5. left=4, right=4. Answer = 4.

Cost: \(O(n \log(\max(\text{piles})))\) — binary search on the range, feasibility check costs \(O(n)\).

Recognition trigger: “minimum/maximum \(X\) such that \(P(X)\) holds” where \(P\) is monotone → binary search on the answer. See the upcoming pattern-triggers post for the trigger row.

D. Comparison sorts

Why · \(O(n \log n)\) is the best possible for comparison-based sorting — any algorithm that only compares elements needs at least \(\Omega(n \log n)\) comparisons in the worst case. Where · whenever you need sorted order and key type supports comparison.

Figure 4 · O(n²) vs O(n log n) — where the crossover happens.

Above n≈10, O(n log n) wins decisively. Below n≈10, insertion sort’s cache-friendly access beats merge sort in practice despite worse asymptotic behaviour.

Running example: [5, 3, 8, 1, 4] for merge sort and quicksort traces.

Merge sort (recursive — see Recursion & Backtracking for the recursion tree): Repeatedly halve the array until each piece has one element (trivially sorted), then merge adjacent sorted pairs back up. Merging two sorted arrays is linear — scan both from the left, always taking the smaller element. The recursion tree has depth \(\log n\), each level doing \(O(n)\) merge work total.

Invariant: after merge, the output array contains the same elements as both halves, in sorted order.

def merge_sort(array):
    if len(array) <= 1:
        return array
    mid = len(array) // 2
    left_half  = merge_sort(array[:mid])
    right_half = merge_sort(array[mid:])
    return merge(left_half, right_half)

def merge(left, right):
    result = []
    while left and right:
        if left[0] <= right[0]:
            result.append(left.pop(0))    # stable: equal elements keep original order
        else:
            result.append(right.pop(0))
    return result + left + right

Trace on [5,3,8,1,4]: split → [5,3] and [8,1,4] → recurse → merge [3,5] with [1,4,8] → [1,3,4,5,8].

Heap sort (uses the heap from Hierarchical Structures): Two phases: first build a min-heap from the array in \(O(n)\); then repeatedly extract the minimum in \(O(\log n)\). The extractions come out in sorted order. No recursion — all work is heap bookkeeping on a flat array.

import heapq

def heap_sort(array):
    heap = array[:]
    heapq.heapify(heap)                   # O(n) build
    return [heapq.heappop(heap) for _ in heap[:]]   # n × O(log n) pops

Trace on [5,3,8,1,4]: heapify → [1,3,8,5,4]. Pops in order: 1, 3, 4, 5, 8 → result [1,3,4,5,8]. (See Hierarchical Structures Section B for the sift-down mechanics.)

Build-heap is \(O(n)\); \(n\) pops cost \(O(n \log n)\) total. In-place variant exists but heapq is cleaner.

Quicksort (recursive — average \(O(n \log n)\), worst \(O(n^2)\) on sorted input): Pick a pivot element, partition the array into three groups — elements smaller than the pivot, equal, and larger — then recurse on the smaller and larger groups. The pivot is in its final sorted position after each partition. Average depth is \(O(\log n)\) with a random pivot; worst case \(O(n)\) depth if the pivot is always the min or max.

Invariant: after partitioning, every element in left is < pivot and every element in right is > pivot — the pivot is in its final position.

def quicksort(array):
    if len(array) <= 1:
        return array
    pivot = array[len(array) // 2]
    left   = [x for x in array if x < pivot]
    middle = [x for x in array if x == pivot]
    right  = [x for x in array if x > pivot]
    return quicksort(left) + middle + quicksort(right)

Trace on [5,3,8,1,4], pivot=8: left=[5,3,1,4], middle=, right=[] → recurse left.

Cost summary:

Sort Time Space Stable Use when
Merge \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n)\) Yes Need stable sort
Heap \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(1)\) No In-place required
Quick \(O(n \log n)\) avg \(O(\log n)\) No Fastest in practice

In practice: use sorted() or list.sort() — Python’s Timsort (hybrid merge + insertion sort, stable, \(O(n \log n)\)) is faster than any manual implementation.

E. Linear sorts

Why · break the \(\Omega(n \log n)\) comparison lower bound by exploiting key structure — \(O(n+k)\) when the key range \(k\) is small. Where · integer keys with bounded range (scores, small IDs); fixed-width strings or integers.

These algorithms don’t compare elements to each other. Instead they use the value itself as an index or bucket address — so the sorted position of an element is computed directly from its value, not derived from comparisons with other elements.

Figure 5 · Counting sort: count → start positions → output.

Three steps on [3,1,2,1,3]: ① count how many of each value appear; ② convert counts to start positions (where each value’s run begins in the output); ③ place each element at its start position.

Counting sort — keys are integers in \([0, k)\):

data = [3, 1, 2, 1, 3]
k = 4                              # keys are 0, 1, 2, 3

counts = [0] * k
for x in data:
    counts[x] += 1                 # count occurrences

output = []
for value, count in enumerate(counts):
    output.extend([value] * count) # place in order
# output: [1, 1, 2, 3, 3]

Cost: \(O(n + k)\) — one pass over the data to fill counts (\(n\)), one pass over the range to emit output (\(k\)). When \(k = O(n)\), this is \(O(n)\).

Figure 6 · Radix sort: two stable passes by digit.

Each pass applies counting sort to one digit (underlined in orange). Sorting least-significant first preserves earlier-digit order across passes — stability is what makes this work.

Radix sort — sort \(d\)-digit numbers digit by digit (least-significant first) using counting sort as the stable inner sort:

def radix_sort(nums, base=10):
    max_digits = len(str(max(nums)))
    for digit in range(max_digits):       # least-significant digit first
        buckets = [[] for _ in range(base)]
        for n in nums:
            buckets[(n // base**digit) % base].append(n)  # shift right by digit positions, take last digit
        nums = [n for bucket in buckets for n in bucket]
    return nums

Trace on [170, 45, 75, 90]: sort by units → [170,90,45,75]; sort by tens → [45,75,90,170]. Each pass is stable, so earlier-digit order is preserved.

Cost: \(O(d \cdot (n + k))\) — \(d\) passes, each a full counting sort costing \(O(n + k)\). For fixed-width integers \(d\) is constant, giving \(O(n)\).

🔗 Connections

  • Loop invariant concept introduced here: Foundations has the general definition.
  • Merge/quicksort build on recursion model: Recursion & Backtracking.
  • Heapsort builds on the heap: Hierarchical Structures.
  • Sorting used in merge intervals and Kruskal’s MST: Array & String Techniques, Graphs.
  • Binary-search-on-answer trigger in the pattern sheet: the upcoming pattern-triggers post.

entry.title: 6. Recursion & Backtracking
entry.content:
The unifying idea. Recursion reduces a problem to a smaller version of itself, hitting a base case to stop. Backtracking is recursion over a choice tree: at each node you pick one option, recurse into it, then undo the pick before trying the next. The template is the same every time; only the base case and the choice set change.

A. Recursion mental model

Why · express solutions that naturally decompose into smaller versions of the same problem. Where · any algorithm that halves or shrinks its input: merge sort, binary search, tree traversal (Graphs).

Every recursive function needs exactly two things: a base case that stops the recursion, and a recursive case that makes the input strictly smaller. If both hold, the function is correct by induction. You never need to trace the full call chain manually.

Example problem: compute \(n!\) (factorial).

Algorithm:

def factorial(n):
    if n == 0:               # base case: stop here
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)   # recursive case: shrink n by 1

factorial(4)   # → 24

Figure 1 · Recursion call stack for factorial(4).

Each frame makes one smaller call until n=0 (orange, base case). The results unwind upward: 1 → 1 → 2 → 6 → 24.

Mechanism trace — factorial(3):

  1. factorial(3): 3 ≠ 0 → call factorial(2).
  2. factorial(2): 2 ≠ 0 → call factorial(1).
  3. factorial(1): 1 ≠ 0 → call factorial(0).
  4. factorial(0): base case → return 1.
  5. Unwind: \(1 \cdot 1 = 1\) → \(2 \cdot 1 = 2\) → \(3 \cdot 2 = 6\).

Cost: \(O(n)\) calls, \(O(n)\) stack space — one frame pushed per recursive call, up to depth \(n\).

Add memoization here → that’s Dynamic Programming, deliberately deferred from this atlas.

[DP expansion — ~4 lines] When subproblems repeat (e.g. fib(3) called multiple times), plain recursion recomputes them. Add a cache: memo = {}; if n in memo: return memo[n]. This is memoization — the top-down form of DP. The call tree becomes a DAG; cost drops from \(O(2^n)\) to \(O(n)\). Bottom-up DP builds the same table iteratively without the call stack overhead.

B. Backtracking template and subsets application

Why · explore every combination of choices without writing nested loops of unknown depth. Where · subsets, permutations, combinations, constraint satisfaction — all are instances of this one template.

Backtracking is DFS over a choice tree (see Graphs for DFS). At each node: choose one option, explore its subtree, unchoose to restore state, then try the next option.

The template (only the base case and choices differ across problems):

results = []

def backtrack(path, choices):
    if base_case(path):           # a complete answer — record it
        results.append(path[:])
        return
    for choice in choices:
        path.append(choice)                         # choose
        backtrack(path, remaining(choices, choice)) # explore
        path.pop()                                  # unchoose

Subsets application

Why · generate all \(2^n\) subsets of a set — the canonical backtracking instance. Where · power sets, feature combinations, any “include or exclude each item” problem.

How subsets differs from the template:

  • No base case guard — record unconditionally at every node, because every path is a valid subset.
  • remaining(choices, choice) = elements after the current index (i + 1) — avoids duplicates.
nums = [1, 2, 3]
results = []

def subsets(start, path):
    results.append(path[:])          # every path is a valid subset
    for i in range(start, len(nums)):
        path.append(nums[i])         # choose nums[i]
        subsets(i + 1, path)         # explore: only later elements
        path.pop()                   # unchoose

subsets(0, [])
# results: [[], [1], [1,2], [1,2,3], [1,3], [2], [2,3], [3]]

Figure 2 · Choice tree for subsets of [1, 2, 3].

Each edge is a choice (+1 = include, skip = exclude). Every path from root to leaf is one subset. Orange leaves are the 8 results — the empty set is the root itself.

Mechanism trace (first branch of Figure 2):

  1. subsets(0, []): record []. Choose 1 → path.
  2. subsets(1, [1]): record. Choose 2 → path [1,2].
  3. subsets(2, [1,2]): record [1,2]. Choose 3 → path [1,2,3].
  4. subsets(3, [1,2,3]): record [1,2,3]. No choices left → return.
  5. Unchoose 3 → [1,2]. Unchoose 2 →. Choose 3 → path [1,3]… and so on.

Cost: \(O(2^n \cdot n)\) — \(2^n\) subsets, each up to \(n\) elements to copy.

[DP expansion — ~3 lines] If you only need to count subsets satisfying a constraint (e.g. “how many subsets sum to target \(T\)?”), backtracking is \(O(2^n)\) but DP is \(O(n \cdot T)\). Subproblems overlap: “can we reach sum \(s\) using items \(0..i\)?” recurs identically from many paths. Cache the answer and the exponential collapse to polynomial.

C. Permutations

Why · generate all \(n!\) orderings of \(n\) items — every item used exactly once. Where · scheduling, anagram generation, any “arrange all items” problem.

Example problem: all permutations of nums = [1, 2, 3].

Difference from subsets: every item is used exactly once, and order matters. Track which items have been used with a used array; recurse until the path is full.

Figure 3 · Permutation tree for [1, 2, 3].

Three choices at the root (any of 1, 2, 3 can go first), two at each second level, one at the third. Six leaves — one per permutation.

Algorithm:

nums = [1, 2, 3]
results = []

def permutations(path, used):
    if len(path) == len(nums):      # all items placed — record
        results.append(path[:])
        return
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        if used[i]:
            continue                # skip already-used items
        used[i] = True
        path.append(nums[i])
        permutations(path, used)
        path.pop()
        used[i] = False

permutations([], [False] * len(nums))
# results: all 6 permutations of [1,2,3]

Mechanism trace (first permutation):

  1. used=[F,F,F]. Choose index 0 (value 1) → path, used=[T,F,F].
  2. Choose index 1 (value 2) → path [1,2], used=[T,T,F].
  3. Choose index 2 (value 3) → path [1,2,3]. Full → record. (Figure 3.)
  4. Unchoose 3, unchoose 2, choose index 2 (value 3) → path [1,3]…

Cost: \(O(n! \cdot n)\) — \(n!\) permutations, each of length \(n\).

D. Combinations

Why · generate all \(\binom{n}{k}\) subsets of exactly size \(k\) — pruning makes it much faster than generating all subsets and filtering. Where · fixed-size selections, \(k\)-element feature sets, any “choose exactly \(k\)” problem.

Example problem: all combinations of size k = 2 from nums = [1, 2, 3].

Difference from subsets: only paths of exactly length k are answers. Pruning: if the remaining elements can’t fill the path to size k, stop early.

Figure 4 · Pruning cuts branches that can’t reach k = 2.

Left: all paths explored without pruning (\(2^3 = 8\) paths). Right: branches marked ✗ are cut because the remaining elements are fewer than still needed — only \(\binom{3}{2} = 3\) paths remain.

Algorithm:

nums = [1, 2, 3]
k = 2
results = []

def combinations(start, path):
    if len(path) == k:              # reached target size — record
        results.append(path[:])
        return
    remaining = len(nums) - start
    needed = k - len(path)
    if remaining < needed:          # can't reach k — prune this branch
        return
    for i in range(start, len(nums)):
        path.append(nums[i])
        combinations(i + 1, path)
        path.pop()

combinations(0, [])
# results: [[1,2], [1,3], [2,3]]

Mechanism trace:

  1. start=0, path=[]. Need 2. Remaining=3. OK → choose 1 → path.
  2. start=1, path=[1]. Need 1. Remaining=2. OK → choose 2 → path [1,2]. Full → record.
  3. Unchoose 2 → choose 3 → path [1,3]. Full → record.
  4. Unchoose 3, unchoose 1 → choose 2 → path. Need 1. Remaining=1. OK → choose 3 → [2,3]. Record.

Cost: \(O\!\left(\binom{n}{k} \cdot k\right)\) with pruning — \(\binom{n}{k}\) valid paths, each of length \(k\) to copy. Without pruning every node in the \(2^n\) subset tree would be visited.

🔗 Connections

  • Recursive cost analysis (master theorem): Foundations.
  • Recursion used in merge sort and quicksort: Sorting & Searching.
  • Backtracking = DFS over a choice tree: Graphs.
  • Backtracking trigger in the pattern sheet: the upcoming pattern-triggers post.

entry.title: 5. Hierarchical Structures
entry.content:
These are the same two memory primitives from Linear Structures, just with a structural invariant added. Three of the four structures are pointer-chained nodes (like a linked list), but the pointers are constrained by an ordering or grouping rule. The heap is different: it is contiguous, like a dynamic array, with no pointers. Without the invariant, you would just have a linked list or a flat array.

Structure Memory primitive Invariant added
BST (Binary Search Tree) Pointer-chained left child < node < right child
Heap Contiguous array parent \(\leq\) children, via index math \(i \to 2i+1,\ 2i+2\)
Trie (prefix tree) Pointer-chained each edge is one character
Union-Find Pointer-chained every pointer leads toward a root; same root = same group

A. BST (Binary Search Tree) — ordered access via a structural invariant

Why · O(log n) find, insert, and delete on a dynamic set of keys. Where · any time you need to maintain a sorted order as items are inserted and deleted: sorted iteration, range queries, next/previous element in sorted order.

A BST is pointer-chained like a linked list, but each node has two pointers instead of one: left for keys smaller than the current node, right for keys larger. At each step you compare the target key to the current node and follow exactly one pointer. That comparison replaces an O(n) scan.

Invariant: every node’s key is greater than all keys in its left subtree and less than all keys in its right subtree. Find becomes a binary decision at each node: go left or go right.

Example problem: maintain a dynamic set of integers with fast find and insert.

Algorithm — find(node, key) and bst_insert(root, key):

def find(node, key):
    if node is None or node.key == key:
        return node
    if key < node.key:
        return find(node.left, key)    # answer must be in left subtree
    return find(node.right, key)       # answer must be in right subtree

def bst_insert(root, key):
    if root is None:
        return Node(key)               # place the new node here
    if key < root.key:
        root.left = bst_insert(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.key:
        root.right = bst_insert(root.right, key)
    return root

# Build the tree: insert 8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 9, 14 (balanced result)
root = None
for k in [8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 9, 14]:
    root = bst_insert(root, k)

Inserting keys in sorted order (e.g. 1, 3, 6, 8) always goes right at every step. No left subtrees ever form, producing the degenerate chain shown on the right of Figure 1.

Figure 1 · BST find path and the cost of imbalance.

Left: balanced BST built from [8,3,10,1,6,9,14]. find(6) takes 3 steps (8→3→6), O(log n). Right: degenerate BST from inserting [1,3,6,8] in sorted order. A right-linked chain, O(n).

Mechanism trace — find(6) in the balanced BST above (root = 8):

  1. 6 < 8 → go left to node 3.
  2. 6 > 3 → go right to node 6.
  3. 6 == 6 → found. 3 comparisons, O(h) where h = tree height.

Why balancing matters: if keys arrive in sorted order, every new node becomes the rightmost child. Height h grows to O(n). A balanced BST (AVL and red-black are two variants) restores height after each insert via local pointer rewirings (rotations), keeping h = O(log n) guaranteed.

Python exposes no balanced BST directly. Use sortedcontainers.SortedList for O(log n) ops.

Costs: find/insert/delete O(log n) balanced · O(n) degenerate · space O(n).

B. Binary heap — ranked access via the heap property

Why · O(log n) push and pop, O(1) peek. The structure you reach for whenever you need to repeatedly extract the minimum (or maximum). Where · top-K problems, scheduling, Dijkstra (Graphs), heapsort (Sorting & Searching).

A heap is contiguous: a dynamic array (same primitive as Section A of Linear Structures). There are no pointers; the tree structure exists only in the index arithmetic.

Invariant: stored as a contiguous array representing a complete binary tree (every level fully filled except the last, which fills left-to-right; this shape is what makes the index math work). Every parent’s value is ≤ its children’s values (min-heap). This means the minimum is always at index 0.

Index arithmetic, for any node at index i:

  • Left child: \(2i + 1\)
  • Right child: \(2i + 2\)
  • Parent: \((i - 1) // 2\)

Figure 2 · Heap array ↔ complete binary tree with index annotations.

The same heap stored as an array (bottom) and drawn as a tree (top). Each edge shows the index formula; the root (index 0) is always the minimum.

Example problem: maintain a collection and repeatedly extract the smallest element.

Algorithm:

import heapq

heap = []
for value in [5, 3, 8]:
    heapq.heappush(heap, value)
# heap = [3, 5, 8], root is always the minimum

minimum = heap[0]              # O(1) peek — no removal
smallest = heapq.heappop(heap) # O(log n) — removes and returns minimum

Figure 3 · Heap push: append then bubble up to restore invariant.

Step 1: append 2 at the end. Step 2: 2 < parent 5 → swap. Step 3: 2 < parent 3 → swap to root. Each swap restores the parent ≤ children invariant one level up.

Mechanism trace — heappush(heap, 2) on [3, 5, 8]:

  1. Append 2 at index 3. Heap = [3, 5, 8, 2].
  2. Parent of index 3 is index 1 (value 5). 2 < 5 → swap. Heap = [3, 2, 8, 5].
  3. Parent of index 1 is index 0 (value 3). 2 < 3 → swap. Heap = [2, 3, 8, 5].
  4. At root. Done (\(O(\log n)\)): height-many swaps.

Mechanism trace — heappop(heap) on [2, 3, 8, 5]:

  1. Swap root (2) with last element (5). Array shrinks: [5, 3, 8]. Root (5) violates invariant.
  2. 5 > smaller child 3 → swap with index 1. Heap = [3, 5, 8].
  3. 5 has no children below. Done: returned 2. Cost: \(O(\log n)\).

Build-heap from an unsorted list: heapq.heapify(a) runs in O(n), not O(n log n). Most nodes are near the bottom and do almost no work: in a 7-node tree, 4 are leaves (0 swaps), 2 are one level up (at most 1 swap each), and only the root does up to 2 swaps. Total: at most 4 swaps for 7 nodes. The deeper the tree, the more nodes are at the bottom where work is cheapest, so the total stays linear in \(n\).

Costs: push/pop O(log n) · peek O(1) · build-heap O(n) · space O(n).

C. Trie — prefix-indexed access

Why · O(L) find and insert where L is the key length, independent of how many keys are stored. Where · autocomplete, spell-check, tokenizers.

A trie stores strings by breaking them into individual characters. To store “cat” you create a path of nodes connected by character steps: root →c→ →a→ →t→ end. Searching for the prefix “ca” follows c then a, two steps regardless of how many words are stored.

Invariant: each edge is labelled with a single character; the path from root to any node spells a prefix shared by all keys in that subtree. Finding a key means following its characters one by one.

Example problem: store a set of words and answer prefix queries (“do any words start with ‘ca’?”).

Algorithm:

trie = {}

def trie_insert(word):
    node = trie
    for char in word:
        if char not in node:
            node[char] = {}        # new child dict for this character
        node = node[char]          # move into the child
    node["END"] = True             # mark end of word

def search_prefix(prefix):
    node = trie
    for char in prefix:
        if char not in node:
            return False
        node = node[char]                  # descend into the subtree for this character
    return True

for word in ["cat", "car", "card"]:
    trie_insert(word)

# trie now looks like:
# {'c': {'a': {'t': {'END': True},
#              'r': {'END': True,
#                    'd': {'END': True}}}}}
# shared path c→a at the top; branches at 'a' for 't' vs 'r'

search_prefix("ca")    # → True  (c and a both exist in the path)
search_prefix("cb")    # → False (no 'b' key under 'c')

Figure 4 · Trie for cat, car, card — shared prefix c→a.

Nodes are anonymous — only the edges carry characters. Orange nodes mark word boundaries (END). The prefix c→a is stored once and shared by all three words. Lookup costs O(L) in the key length.

Mechanism trace — trie_insert("car") after "cat" already exists:

Before: trie = {'c': {'a': {'t': {'END': True}}}}

  1. 'c' in trie → descend. Current node = trie['c'] = {'a': {'t': {'END': True}}}.
  2. 'a' in node → descend. Current node = {'t': {'END': True}}.
  3. 'r' not in node → create it. Node becomes {'t': {'END': True}, 'r': {}}.
  4. Mark end. Node 'r' becomes {'END': True}.

After: trie = {'c': {'a': {'t': {'END': True}, 'r': {'END': True}}}}

Only 1 new node created. The shared prefix c→a cost nothing extra.

Costs: search/insert \(O(L)\) (\(L\) = key length, one \(O(1)\) dict lookup per character) · space \(O(\Sigma \cdot L_{\max} \cdot n)\) worst case (\(\Sigma\) = alphabet size, e.g. 26 for lowercase letters) but shared prefixes reduce this significantly.

D. Union-Find — group membership via parent pointers

Why · near-O(1) per operation to track which group an element belongs to, across many merges. Where · merging duplicate records (entity resolution), clustering, Kruskal’s Minimum Spanning Tree algorithm (Graphs), connected components.

Union-Find is pointer-chained like a linked list, but every pointer points upward toward a representative called the root. Instead of a next field in each node, there is one flat parent array: parent[i] is the parent of element i. A root has parent[root] == root (it points to itself).

Invariant: following any element’s parent pointers reaches a root. Two elements are in the same group if and only if they reach the same root.

Figure 5 · Union-Find: initial state, after two merges, after path compression.

Panel 1: each element is its own root (all self-loops). Panel 2: after union(0,1) and union(1,2), the chain 0→1→2 forms one group; node 3 is alone. Panel 3: find(0) shortcuts 0 directly to root 2 (orange, path compression). The next find(0) costs one hop.

Example problem: given “connect A to B” operations, answer “are A and B in the same group?”

Algorithm:

parent = [0, 1, 2, 3]   # each element its own representative

def find(x):
    if parent[x] != x:
        parent[x] = find(parent[x])   # path compression
    return parent[x]

def union(x, y):
    root_x, root_y = find(x), find(y)
    if root_x != root_y:
        parent[root_x] = root_y

union(0, 1)
union(1, 2)
# parent = [1, 2, 2, 3]  — groups: {0,1,2} and {3}

find(0) == find(2)   # True
find(0) == find(3)   # False

Mechanism trace — same 4 elements as the figure:

  1. union(0,1): root of 0 is 0, root of 1 is 1; set parent[0] = 1. (Figure panel 2, step 1.)
  2. union(1,2): root of 1 is 1, root of 2 is 2; set parent[1] = 2. Chain: 0→1→2. (Panel 2.)
  3. find(0): follow 0→1→2. parent[2]==2, stop. Path compression sets parent[0] = 2. (Panel 3.)
  4. Next find(0): one hop to root 2. O(1).

Costs: find/union \(O(\alpha(n))\) amortized · space \(O(n)\).

\(\alpha\) is the inverse Ackermann function. The Ackermann function grows absurdly fast, faster than any practical formula, so its inverse barely budges. \(\alpha(n) \leq 4\) for any \(n\) below \(A(4,4)\), a number with more digits than atoms in the observable universe. Mathematically it is not \(O(1)\), but you will never see it exceed 4.

Why nearly \(O(1)\): each node moves closer to the root at most once per level it traverses; after compression it points directly to the root and never contributes to a long path again. The total traversal work across all operations is bounded, giving \(O(\alpha(n))\) amortized rather than \(O(\log n)\).

🔗 Connections

  • Master map and cost table: Overview.
  • Heap used in Dijkstra and graph MST algorithms: Graphs.
  • Heap used in heapsort: Sorting & Searching.
  • Trie and Union-Find as recognition triggers: the upcoming pattern-triggers post.

entry.title: 4. Array & String Techniques
entry.content:
The unifying idea. Every technique here replaces re-examining the whole array on every step with maintaining a claim about the current state — an invariant — and updating it in \(O(1)\) per step. Name the invariant and you can both trust the algorithm and often derive the code from it.

A. Two pointers

Why · \(O(n)\) with \(O(1)\) space for problems with a two-ended structure. Where · “find a pair,” “compare ends,” “shrink from both sides” — the upcoming pattern-triggers post trigger row.

Trigger: two quantities are at either end of a sorted array or string, and moving one end is always the right choice.

Invariant: if an answer exists, it lies within the index range [left, right] — so advancing the pointer that cannot improve the answer never misses a solution.

Example problem: given an array of wall heights, find the two walls that enclose the maximum water area.

Algorithm:

heights = [1, 8, 3, 7]
left, right = 0, len(heights) - 1
best = 0
while left < right:
    area = min(heights[left], heights[right]) * (right - left)
    best = max(best, area)
    if heights[left] <= heights[right]:  # shorter wall limits area — move it
        left += 1
    else:
        right -= 1
# The formula and the if-condition change per problem; the while-loop structure stays.

Figure 1 · Two pointers converging: move the shorter wall.

The shorter wall limits the area — moving it is the only step that could possibly find something better, so the invariant is preserved.

Mechanism trace — Container With Most Water, heights = [1, 8, 3, 7]:

  1. left = 1, right = 7: area = 1 × 3 = 3. Left shorter → move left inward.
  2. left = 8, right = 7: area = 7 × 2 = 14. Right shorter → move right inward.
  3. left = 8, right = 3: area = 3 × 1 = 3. Converged. Best = 14.

Each step is \(O(1)\); at most \(n\) steps → O(n) total.

Variant — fast/slow pointer (Floyd’s cycle): fast moves 2 steps, slow moves 1; they meet if and only if a cycle exists. Lives on Graphs.

Costs: \(O(n)\) time · \(O(1)\) space.

B. Sliding window

Why · \(O(n)\) for any “longest/shortest subarray satisfying a constraint” problem. Where · substrings, subarrays, rate-limiting windows in streaming data (the upcoming DSA-at-work post).

Trigger: “longest/shortest subarray or substring satisfying a constraint.”

Invariant: the window [left, right] always satisfies the constraint. On each step: expand right (add one element); if the constraint breaks, shrink left until it holds again.

Example problem: given a string, find the longest substring with no repeated character.

Algorithm:

seen = {}   # tracks last index of each character
left = 0
best = 0
for right, char in enumerate(a):
    if char in seen and seen[char] >= left:  # char is already in the window
        left = seen[char] + 1               # shrink: move left past the duplicate
    seen[char] = right
    best = max(best, right - left + 1)       # window [left..right] has no repeats

Figure 2 · Sliding window expanding and shrinking.

Each row is one state. The window (blue) expands right until a repeat forces a left shrink, then expands again. Each element enters and leaves at most once.

Mechanism trace — longest substring without repeating characters, s = "abcbad":

right char action window len
0 a expand "a" 1
1 b expand "ab" 2
2 c expand "abc" 3
3 b repeat → shrink left to 2 "cb" 2
4 a expand "cba" 3
5 d expand "cbad" 4 ← answer

Costs: \(O(n)\) — each element enters and leaves the window at most once.

C. Prefix / suffix sums

Why · \(O(1)\) per range query after an \(O(n)\) build — the same idea powers the “product except self” trick. Where · repeated range aggregates, cumulative statistics, “product of all except self.”

Trigger: “answer a range sum/product query many times” or “need aggregate of all elements except position \(i\).”

Invariant: prefix[i] = aggregate of a[0..i-1]. Range query [start, end] = prefix[end+1] - prefix[start] — one subtraction, no scan.

Example problem: given an array, answer many “sum of elements from index start to end” queries in O(1) each.

Algorithm:

a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9]
n = len(a)

# Build prefix array — O(n)
prefix = [0] * (n + 1)
for i in range(n):
    prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + a[i]   # prefix[i] = sum of a[0..i-1]

# Answer any range query — O(1)
def range_sum(start, end):
    return prefix[end + 1] - prefix[start]   # sum of a[start..end]

range_sum(2, 5)   # → 19  (= 4+1+5+9)

Figure 3 · Prefix array and O(1) range query.

Top row: original values (orange = queried range). Bottom row: prefix sums. The query resolves to one subtraction between two highlighted prefix cells.

Mechanism trace — a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9], query sum of a[2..5]:

Build the prefix array once, then answer in O(1):

i a[i] prefix[i+1] = prefix[i] + a[i]
0 3 3
1 1 4
2 4 8
3 1 9
4 5 14
5 9 23

range_sum(2, 5) = prefix[6] - prefix[2] = 23 - 4 = 19 = 4+1+5+9 ✓

Variant — Product of Array Except Self. Run prefix products left-to-right and suffix products right-to-left; result[i] = prefix[i] × suffix[i]. O(n), no division needed.

Costs: \(O(n)\) build — one pass to fill the prefix array · \(O(1)\) per query — one subtraction.

D. Merge intervals

Why · \(O(n \log n)\) to merge all overlapping spans in one sorted sweep. Where · calendar/booking systems, sessionization, rate-limit windows (the upcoming DSA-at-work post).

Trigger: “merge overlapping ranges,” “find gaps,” “detect conflicts in time spans.”

Invariant: sort by start; the current interval overlaps the last merged one if and only if curr.start ≤ last.end. If it does, extend last.end; otherwise start a new merged span.

Example problem: given a list of time intervals, merge all overlapping ones.

Algorithm:

intervals = [[1, 3], [2, 6], [8, 10]]
intervals.sort(key=lambda interval: interval[0])   # sort by start time
merged = [intervals[0]]
for start, end in intervals[1:]:
    if start <= merged[-1][1]:                     # overlaps last merged span
        merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], end)    # extend it
    else:
        merged.append([start, end])                # disjoint: start a new span
# merged → [[1, 6], [8, 10]]

Figure 4 · Merge intervals: before and after.

Top: original intervals, orange pair overlaps. Bottom: merged result — overlapping spans combined, disjoint spans kept separate.

Mechanism trace — [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10]]:

  1. intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) → [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10]].
  2. Start with [1,3]. Next [2,6]: \(2 \leq 3\) → overlap → extend to [1,6].
  3. Next [8,10]: \(8 > 6\) → no overlap → append. Result: [[1,6],[8,10]].

Costs: \(O(n \log n)\) (sort dominates) · \(O(n)\) space.

E. Bit tricks

Why · \(O(1)\) per operation for problems involving counting bits, pairing, or set membership. Where · duplicate detection, bitmasked state, performance-critical loops.

Trigger: “find the element without a pair,” “count set bits,” “check if a number is a power of two.”

Bit basics (everything below follows from these):

  • A number is stored as binary digits. Each position \(i\) (from right, starting at 0) has weight \(2^i\). So \(6 = 110_2 = 1{\cdot}2^2 + 1{\cdot}2^1 + 0{\cdot}2^0 = 4+2+0\) and \(5 = 101_2 = 1{\cdot}2^2 + 0{\cdot}2^1 + 1{\cdot}2^0 = 4+0+1\).
  • AND (&): bit is 1 only if both inputs are 1. 0b110 & 0b101 = 0b100 (=4).
  • OR (|): bit is 1 if either input is 1. 0b110 | 0b101 = 0b111 (=7).
  • XOR (^): bit is 1 if inputs differ. 0b110 ^ 0b101 = 0b011 (=3). Same bits cancel: x ^ x = 0.
  • -x in binary (two’s complement): to negate a number, flip all bits then add 1. Step by step for \(x = 6\): 0110 (start) → 1001 (flip all bits) → 1010 (add 1) = \(-6\). Compare: \(x = \mathtt{0110}\), \(-x = \mathtt{1010}\) — bit 1 (value 2) is set in both. The lowest set bit always survives negation. That is why x & (-x) isolates it.

Trick 1 — XOR: identical values cancel. Follows directly from the XOR definition above: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, so every pair cancels and only the unique value survives.

nums = [2, 3, 2, 5, 5]   # every value appears twice except 3
result = 0
for v in nums:
    result ^= v   # pairs cancel; singleton survives
# result → 3

Trace: 0^2=2 → 2^3=1 → 1^2=3 → 3^5=6 → 6^5=3 ✓

Cost: \(O(n)\) time · \(O(1)\) space.

Trick 2 — x & (x-1) clears the lowest set bit. Subtracting 1 from x flips the lowest set bit and all bits below it (borrow chain in binary); AND with the original keeps only the bits above it.

Figure 5 · x & (x−1): how subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit.

Three rows: x, x−1, and x&(x−1). The orange bit (lowest set bit) and everything below it flip in x−1; AND with x clears them.

x = 0b10110100   # 180: has 4 set bits
count = 0
while x:
    x &= x - 1   # clear one set bit per iteration
    count += 1   # count = 4 after the loop
# Also: x & (x-1) == 0 iff x is a power of two (only one set bit)

Cost: \(O(k)\) where \(k\) = number of set bits — faster than scanning all bits.

Trick 3 — x & (-x) isolates the lowest set bit. Negating x (flip all bits, add 1) preserves the lowest set bit while flipping everything above it. AND keeps only the bit set in both.

Figure 6 · x & (−x): the lowest set bit survives negation.

x = 6 (0110) and −x = 10 (1010) share only bit 1; AND isolates it — result = 2 (0010).

x = 6             # binary: 0110 — lowest set bit is bit 1 (value 2)
lsb = x & (-x)    # → 2  (binary: 0010)

Used in Fenwick trees (Hierarchical Structures) for index arithmetic.

Cost: \(O(1)\) — single arithmetic operation.

🔗 Connections

  • Linear structures these techniques operate on: Linear Structures.
  • Invariant concept (init / maintain / terminate): Sorting & Searching.
  • Technique recognition triggers and work applications: the upcoming pattern-triggers post / the upcoming DSA-at-work post.
  • Floyd’s cycle (fast/slow pointer variant of two pointers): Graphs.
  • Fenwick tree (uses bit trick x & (-x)): Hierarchical Structures.
